Now I have substantial material. Let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I have read.

---

# Exodus 15 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## The Song of Moses (vv. 1–18)

### v. 1 — "Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD…"

**Traditional Reading:**
- This is the first sacred song recorded in Scripture and "in some respects it is first in merit as well as in time" (Spurgeon). It likely came spontaneously as Moses led the nation into the wilderness after crossing the Red Sea. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Ellicott notes that with his characteristic modesty, Moses does not say he composed it, but it is "scarcely conceivable that it can have had any other author." It bears close resemblance to Egyptian religious poetry, with which Moses would have been familiar from his early training. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Gill observes this song is typical/typological: Moses (the deliverer) is a type of Christ, and Israel a type of the spiritual Israel redeemed by Christ. The whole chapter points to the "song of Moses and the Lamb" in Revelation 15:3. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/15.htm
- The song is entirely about God. "Notice, the song is all of God; there is not a word about Moses. Read this song through, and neither Moses, nor Aaron, nor Miriam are in it: God is all in all" (Spurgeon). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Guzik (Enduring Word): "One great principle of worship is that it is unto the LORD, not unto man. When we worship God in song, our audience is the LORD Himself and not the people around us." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Precept Austin adds that this follows Exodus 14:31 — "When Israel saw the great power…the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD." Then they sang. The psalmist comments: "Then they believed His words. They sang His praise" (Ps 106:12). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-15-commentary

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik):**
- "God prizes these spontaneous expressions of praise and worship. This was a new song sung unto the LORD (as in Psalm 40:3)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes, cited at Precept Austin):**
- The song falls into three sections: praise to God (vv. 1b–3), the cause for the praise (vv. 4–13), and the conclusion (vv. 14–18). It is "very much like the other declarative praise psalms – the resolve to praise, the power of God, the victory over the enemies, the incomparability of God in his redemption, and the fear of the people." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-15-commentary

---

### v. 2 — "The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation…"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott notes the Hebrew uses the contracted form of Jehovah — "Jah" — for the first time in Scripture, for the sake of rhythm. "My strength and song is Jah." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Spurgeon: "Note, the word is not 'The Lord gives me strength,' but 'The Lord is my strength'! How strong is a believer? I say it with reverence, he is as strong as God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- "He has become my salvation" recognises we cannot save ourselves — God must become our salvation. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Gill elaborates: Christ "is not only their Saviour, but salvation itself; being not only the author of it…but made that itself unto them, even their all in all." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/15.htm
- Ellicott on "I will prepare him an habitation": The KJV rendering is disputed. The LXX, Vulgate and most moderns translate "I will glorify him." The law of parallelism requires a meaning like "glorify" to match "exalt" in the next clause. Also, Moses would not yet have had the idea of building God a dwelling before the Sinai revelation (Exodus 25–27). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

**Reformed Baptist (Desiring God):**
- "But God is more than our salvation. In fact, if he is not also our song, he is not our salvation. … When we stand before the cross, with dry and safe ground under our feet, it would be outrageous to remain silent." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-parted-the-seas-for-you

---

### v. 3 — "The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is His name."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott: "The directness and boldness of the anthropomorphism is markedly archaic, and is wisely retained by our translators." The LXX weakens this to "crusher of wars" — the Hebrew is bolder. In the very name Jehovah is implied all might; the name meaning "the Existent" implies that nothing else has any real existence independently of Him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Gill (christologically): "'A man,' which has respect to the future incarnation of Christ…He is not a common man of war or warrior; He is the Captain of the Lord's host, the Leader and Commander of the people, the Generalissimo of the armies in heaven and earth." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/15.htm

---

### vv. 4–5 — "Pharaoh's chariots and army He has cast into the sea… they sank…like a stone."

**Traditional Reading:**
- These verses form the close of the first stanza. The Israelites focus on the one great fact of deliverance through destruction of the Egyptians. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Gill sees the drowning of the "chosen captains" as an emblem of the destruction of antichrist and all antichristian states. Pharaoh and his host were types of these. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/15.htm

---

### vv. 6–7 — "Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power… shattered the enemy… Your burning wrath consumed them like stubble."

**Traditional Reading:**
- The "right hand" is an anthropomorphism representing God's skill and power. This phrase is used more than fifty times in Scripture (Psalm 45:4; 48:10; 110:1; Ephesians 1:20, etc.). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Ellicott: This is the second anthropomorphism in the song, "following naturally on the first, and occurring in the later Scriptures frequently, though now used for the first time." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- The imagery of "stubble" consumed by wrath is repeated elsewhere (Isaiah 51:20) — God's wrath is like fire and the wicked are as chaff. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/15.htm

---

### v. 8 — "At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up; like a wall the currents stood firm…"

**Traditional Reading:**
- This poetic description matches the "strong east wind" of Exodus 14:21. Ellicott warns against wooden literalism: "The literalism which, taking its stand on these phrases, maintains that the water 'gave up its nature' … indicates an inability to distinguish poetry from prose, and fact from imagery." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Gill notes the "blast of thy nostrils" indicates how easily God accomplished this — as effortlessly as a man breathing. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/15.htm

**Reformed Baptist (Desiring God):**
- "Waves don't pile up. Floods don't hold back. Seas don't stand still. Unless God blows his nose. He drove back miles of raging water with a breath from his nose." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-parted-the-seas-for-you

---

### v. 9 — "The enemy declared, 'I will pursue, I will overtake…'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gill notes the staccato phrasing without the conjunction "and" in the Hebrew shows "the passion he was in, the hastiness of his expressions, and the eagerness of his mind." Each "I will" reflects "the fixed resolution and determination he had made." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/15.htm
- Ellicott: The soldiers were as eager as Pharaoh. Their particular passion was cupidity — desire for the rich spoil (gold, silver, apparel, flocks) the Israelites carried from Egypt. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

### v. 10 — "But You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead…"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott supplies a historical detail beyond Exodus 14: a second wind from the opposite direction hastened the waters' return. "As a strong east wind had driven the waters…to the north-westward, so (it would seem) their return was aided and hastened by a wind from the opposite direction." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- The heavy armour of the picked warriors caused them to sink like lead — an eye-witness detail. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

### v. 11 — "Who among the gods is like You, O LORD? Who is like You—majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders?"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott: This verse highlights three points on which Jehovah is unapproachable — holiness, awefulness, and miraculous power. "The gods of the heathen were, in fact, either nonentities or evil spirits." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Guzik: "Worship should proclaim the superiority of the LORD God over anything else that claims to be god." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- At Precept Austin, John MacArthur comments on God being "glorious in holiness" as a central truth about His character. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-15-commentary

**Baptist (GTY – MacArthur):**
- MacArthur, referencing this verse, teaches: "The beauty of the Lord is the beauty of holiness. I don't think we understand the holiness of God." — https://www.gty.org/sermons/GTY58/the-forgotten-side-of-god

---

### v. 12 — "You stretched out Your right hand, and the earth swallowed them up."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott: This concentrates "into four words the gist" of the two previous stanzas. "The sea, which actually 'swallowed them,' was a part of the earth." He cautions against literalism creating false discrepancies with vv. 4–5 and 10. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

### v. 13 — "With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed…guide them to Your holy dwelling."

**Traditional Reading:**
- This verse opens Part II of the song — the forward-looking, prophetic section (vv. 13–18). Ellicott says the verbs are best read as presents: "leadest forth…guidest." The guidance was just beginning. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- "Your holy habitation" — Ellicott thinks Moses knew more than just Canaan generally; he "certainly knew that when Canaan was reached God would select a place to 'put His name there'" (cf. Deuteronomy 12:5), and possibly knew by revelation which place that would be. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

### vv. 14–16 — "The nations will hear and tremble… Philistia… Edom… Moab… Canaan… as still as a stone until Your people pass by…"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott says this predicts the actual fear that fell on the peoples — see Numbers 22:3 (Moab), Joshua 2:11 and 5:1 (Canaan), Joshua 9:3–15 (Gibeonites). Rahab later testified: "we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea for you" (Joshua 2:10). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Guzik: "Fear and dread will fall on them… Some forty years later Rahab the prostitute from Jericho told the Israeli spies" exactly this. "The people of Canaan did hear of what God did for Israel and some responded with godly fear." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- "Till Your people pass by" refers to crossing the frontier into Canaan. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

### v. 17 — "You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance… the sanctuary, O Lord, Your hands have established."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott: The "mountain of Your inheritance" is Canaan generally — a land consisting almost entirely of mountains, with only two significant plains (Sharon and Esdraelon). The "Sanctuary" is the place where God would put His name, spoken of as already "made" and "established" because it was so in the Divine counsels. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

### v. 18 — "The LORD will reign forever and ever!"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott calls this "the sublime utterance, beyond which no thought of man can go." Compare Psalm 10:16; 29:10; 145:13; 146:10. "In simplicity and consequent force the expression of the idea by Moses transcends all later ones." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Guzik: "After such a great victory we can sense that Israel really believed this, and they were really ready to let the LORD reign over them. This state of victory and surrender did not last very long." Yet the truth endures. The Song of Moses echoes to Revelation 15:3–4. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Precept Austin (quoting John Phillips): "The song of Moses commemorated the execution of the foe, the expectation of the saints, and the exaltation of the Lord; the song of the Lamb deals with the same three themes." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-15-commentary

---

### v. 19 — Prose summary: Pharaoh's forces destroyed; Israel walked on dry ground.

**Traditional Reading:**
- Ellicott: This verse is parenthetic, not part of the song. It is an historical comment appended when the song was a separate document, emphasising "the great fact of Israel's final deliverance—the nucleus around which Exodus gathers itself." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

### vv. 20–21 — "Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine…all the women followed her…"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Miriam is the first woman in the Bible called a "prophetess." She is identified as Aaron's sister (rather than Moses') because Aaron was the head of the family. She is almost certainly the sister who watched the infant Moses in the bulrushes (Exodus 2:3–8). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Ellicott notes the Egyptian custom: "The arrangement of the choir on this occasion into two bands—one of males, the other of females—and the combined employment of music, song, and dancing by the female band, are in close accord with Egyptian customs." Timbrels (tambourines) were favourite instruments in Egypt, typically played by women. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Miriam and the women sang the refrain at the close of each stanza of the song. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Guzik notes that Miriam later used her leadership position unwisely to challenge Moses' authority (Numbers 12). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/

**Baptist (GTY – MacArthur):**
- MacArthur on Miriam: "She is called a prophetess because through her God revealed messages for His people. She is the first woman in the Bible to be given that privilege." — https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-389/miriam-the-leading-lady-of-the-exodus

**On Dancing in Worship:**
- Ellicott observes that dancing "though adopted into religious worship by many nations, sanctioned by the present passage, by the example of David (2Samuel 6:16), and by expressions in the Psalms (Psalm 149:3; 150:4), has never found an entrance into Christian ceremonial, unless among a few fanatic sects. The reason…is to be found in the abuses which, through human infirmity, became by degrees connected with the practice." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm

---

## The Journey to Marah and Elim (vv. 22–27)

### v. 22 — Three days in the Desert of Shur without water.

**Traditional Reading:**
- The Wilderness of Shur is the arid tract extending from Lake Serbônis southwards. The Israelites traversed the southern portion — an actual desert, treeless and waterless. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Guzik: "Three days is not a very long time. But it is long enough to forget the great victory and power of God." Also notes Buckingham's observation: "Three days is the maximum time the human body can go without water in the desert." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik): "The Egyptians found enough water, and even too much of it, for they were drowned in the sea, but the well-beloved Israelites had no water at all. So is it with the wicked man; he often has enough of wealth, and too much of it, till he is drowned in sensual delights and perishes in floods of prosperity." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/

---

### vv. 23–25a — Bitter waters at Marah sweetened by a tree.

**Traditional Reading:**
- Marah means "bitter." The extreme bitterness of the springs at the southern end of the Wilderness of Shur is witnessed by all modern travellers (Burckhardt, Robinson, Wellsted). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Moses cried to the LORD and was shown a tree (not his rod — Spurgeon notes: "I think, if I had been there, I should have suggested that Moses should use that rod of his. … Oh, yes, you know, we are always for running to old methods! But God is a Sovereign, and he will work as he pleases.") — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- A possible natural explanation: chemicals in the sap of the broken limb drew mineral content to the bottom of the pools, leaving good water on top (Buckingham, cited by Guzik). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- "God was not only interested in getting the children of Israel out of Egypt, He also wanted to get Egypt out of the children of Israel — both physically and spiritually." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Medieval commentators saw the tree as a type of the cross, "by which the bitterest of life's waters is sweetened" (Cole). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/

---

### vv. 25b–26 — "There He made for them a statute and an ordinance… He tested them… 'I am the LORD who heals you.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- God took advantage of the occasion to draw a lesson: as He had healed the waters, so if Israel would faithfully keep His commandments, He would "heal" them, keeping them free from Egypt's diseases. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/15.htm
- Guzik: "God tested Israel by giving them a command to obey. When God tells us what to do, He really gives us a test. Our obedience determines if we pass the test or not." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Dr. S.I. McMillen in *None of These Diseases* noted that many of God's laws (circumcision, quarantine, washing, kosher eating) had direct medical benefits for Israel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- "This miracle was connected with a promise; viz., from now on obedience to commands and statutes would bring healing, both physically and morally" (Kaiser). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Jehovah-Rapha ("the LORD who heals you") is revealed as a new name for God at Marah. Guzik: "Marah was a place of bitterness and testing, but because Israel endured and received provision from God, they genuinely gained…They learned prayer, they learned self-distrust, they learned daily dependence, they learned obedience, and they even learned a new name for God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):**
- The physical health promise ("none of the diseases…which I have brought on the Egyptians") is understood by Guzik as directly tied to obedience. Beyond medical implications, "obedience also means we are at peace with God – and free from a tremendous amount of stress and anxiety in life. This has an obvious benefit to the health of any person." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/

---

### v. 27 — Elim: twelve springs and seventy palm trees.

**Traditional Reading:**
- After testing came refreshing. "He knew exactly what they needed, and He knew when to test them and when to rest them." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/
- Spurgeon noted a significant contrast: "Israel had no miracle at Elim. Wells and palm trees they had; but they had no miracle there, no miraculous change of the bitter into the sweet; and they had no statute, and no ordinance, and no promise, and no new revelation of God, and no new name for Jehovah there." The greater spiritual gain came at Marah. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-15/

---

## Summary of Distinctive Protestant Traditions (Where They Differ)

On this chapter, the major Protestant traditions do not show sharp doctrinal divergence. The differences are mainly in **emphasis** rather than competing interpretations:

| Tradition | Emphasis in Exodus 15 |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Reformed Baptist (Spurgeon/Desiring God)** | God's sovereignty in deliverance; Christ-centred typology; worship as response to sovereign grace. Spurgeon stresses "God is all in all." |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – Guzik)** | Spontaneous praise; the power of the new song; physical healing (Jehovah-Rapha); testing as revealing true spiritual condition. |
| **Conservative Evangelical/Baptist (GTY – MacArthur)** | God's holiness ("glorious in holiness"); Miriam as first prophetess; the song extolling God's power and supremacy. |
| **Anglican/Classic (Ellicott)** | Literary and historical analysis; the song's structure; Egyptian cultural parallels; caution against wooden literalism with poetic imagery. |
| **Older Reformed (Gill)** | Thorough typology — every detail points to Christ, the church, and antichrist's defeat. The Song of Moses prefigures the Song of the Lamb. |

**On "The LORD is a warrior" (v. 3):** Gill reads this Christologically (pointing to Christ's incarnation and role as divine warrior), while Ellicott focuses on the boldness of the archaic anthropomorphism. Both traditions affirm the same God, but Gill's Baptist covenantal typology drives him to find Christ in every phrase, whereas Ellicott's Anglican approach is more restrained and literary.

**On the dancing (vv. 20–21):** Ellicott notes that dancing "has never found an entrance into Christian ceremonial, unless among a few fanatic sects." This reflects a traditional Anglican/Lutheran reserve. Pentecostal and charismatic traditions, by contrast, would be more open to dance in worship, citing this very passage as precedent — though this specific debate was not explicitly found in the pages searched.

**On healing (v. 26):** The Pentecostal/charismatic reading (Guzik) draws attention to physical healing promises. The broader evangelical reading (Precept Austin, Kaiser) treats the healing promise as both physical and moral, conditioned on covenant obedience. No prosperity gospel or Word of Faith sources were found in the permitted sites for this chapter.
